title: Many tellings, one Rama
hookLine: two herb flights become one picture, and one line of a hymn
carry: many tellings, one rama, kept alive by reciting
last: NISHKAMA KARMA: DO THE WORK, DON'T CLAIM THE PRIZE.

cards: On a roadside shrine in North India, on the wall of a truck stop, in a grandmother's prayer room, the same picture keeps turning up: Hanuman in flight, mace in one hand, a mountain balanced on the other.
Ask someone what's happening in it, and they'll probably tell a slightly different story from the one you've just heard. Lakshmana is dying. There's a physician.
There's a deadline at dawn. That version is real too, and here's where it comes from.

teach.b: Valmiki actually tells a herb flight twice. The first is the one you've followed: after Indrajit's Brahma weapon, the whole army down, Jambavan sending Hanuman north.
The second comes near the very end of the war, when Lakshmana alone is struck by a spear, and Sushena, the monkey physician, sends Hanuman for the herbs again.
Over time, in popular memory, the two have flowed together into one: Lakshmana wounded, the physician, the flight, the mountain, the race against the dawn. Later poets shaped that memory too.

The Hanuman Chalisa, a hymn to Hanuman that devotees recite, often on Tuesdays and Saturdays, says it in one line: he brought the life-giving herb, and Lakshmana lived, and Rama embraced him with joy.
For some people that line is the whole story, even if they've never opened Valmiki. So which is right? Both belong to the tradition.
Hindus have never had just one Ramayana. There's Valmiki's Sanskrit, Kamban's Tamil, Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas in Awadhi, and many more, told, sung and acted across India and beyond.
Each keeps the heart; here, Hanuman as the one who brings healing, against the clock, when everyone else is helpless.
And the story lives less on a shelf than in the reciting, which is one reason people say the Chalisa when someone they love is in hospital.

how: Devotees of Hanuman recite the Hanuman Chalisa, often on Tuesdays and Saturdays, and images of Hanuman carrying the mountain hang in homes, temples and shops; people pray to him for the recovery of the sick.

s: Valmiki tells only one herb flight
he tells two: one for the whole army, one later for Lakshmana.
the Hanuman Chalisa mentions the herb that saved Lakshmana
one line says he brought the herb and Lakshmana lived.
the popular picture of Hanuman with the mountain is wrong
it's how the later tradition remembers him; Valmiki just tells it in two parts.

games.q: you're a storyteller with one evening to tell the herb story. Valmiki has two flights. what do you do?
o: tell both, exactly as Valmiki has them.
tell one, with Lakshmana at the center.
games.why: over time, tellers did exactly that, which is why the picture most people know is Lakshmana, the physician and the dawn deadline.

practice: Bring to mind someone who is ill or struggling right now, and picture them gently, with nothing to fix.
If you pray, hold them in prayer in your own way, or say Jai Hanuman for them, as so many families do; if you don't, breathe out slowly toward them, carrying a simple wish for their ease.

wordCard.voice: Hanuman Chalisa. A hymn to Hanuman, recited by devotees, whose line says he brought the life-giving herb and Lakshmana lived, folding two flights into one.

orig.note: Avadhi, from the Hanuman Chalisa: bringing the life-giving herb, you revived Lakhan (Lakshmana).
